stories.summary: OpenAI pledged to solicit community input around AI data centers, publish construction plans and protect ratepayers.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
sources.text: OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI. The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws. "What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward." Other tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic , have outlined several similar commitments . On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI. AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio . OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then. "Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said. sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built. It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies. The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects. OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays. It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC. Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions. The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions. OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress. Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. sources.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
sources.text: The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments. The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments. Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion , OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials. Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects. OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers ) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

sources.name: MIT Technology Review AI
sources.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
sources.text: Some of the largest AI infrastructure projects in the world are underway in Texas. A dramatic political shift could slow their construction—and deepen concerns about the economics of the AI boom. Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself. Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere. It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red. This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices. Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it. sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: AI stocks hammered by midterm shock as data center buildout becomes a 'war of attrition'
sources.text: This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here. The Democrats' stunning rout of the Republicans during the midterms this week wasn't just a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump , but also a potential roadblock to huge plans to build artificial intelligence data centers across the country. Since the landmark results came in, tech and AI stocks have been jolted by market volatility. The most valuable tech companies in the U.S. and Europe were hit with a massive sell-off on Thursday as investors got nervous. Nvidia lost 9.3%, with AMD shedding 17.3%, Microsoft 3.6%, Micron 17.5%, Broadcom 10.4%, Tesla 10.8% and SpaceX 9.1%. Neoclouds, which rely on their ability to serve AI computing power and are involved in massive data center projects, were also hit particularly hard. Nebius dropped 15%, Iren fell 17% and CoreWeave 10% on Thursday. By Friday morning, U.S. tech stocks were showing signs of recovery, but the market blip is a warning of potentially rougher roads ahead for the AI boom in America. "The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom," wrote Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com in a note on Thursday after the bell. There were dozens of local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, CNBC reported on Wednesday. "The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations," said Rodda. Earnings season had been an "overall disappointment" for the markets, he added, with Magnificent Seven results so far "undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down." Now, Rodda wrote, the risk that the investment boom could be slowed further "by measures as potentially disruptive as moratoriums on new data center construction, investors are rushing to the exits on so-called AI trades." Opposition to data centers in the U.S. is a long-standing issue. Between January 2024 and May 2026, at least 46 AI data center projects across 20 U.S. states, representing more than $170 billion in announced investment, were blocked, withdrawn or stalled following community opposition, according to research carried out by think tank International Data Center Authority, or IDCA. The midterms will weigh on investors' minds, Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…the answer in our view is a clear YES," he wrote. Democrats taking control, particularly over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI over the next two years, Ives added. The figures floating around on the scale of projected AI infrastructure spending are eye-watering. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across computing, data centers and power. But, heading into the election, AI stocks were already looking shaky on Wall Street. Chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies sold off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. Many hyperscalers have turned cash flow negative as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure. "AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it," said Dominique Toublan, head of U.S. credit strategy at Barclays Investment Bank, in a note from Wednesday. "The AI race shifts from a prisoner's dilemma to a war of attrition: scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets." By Thursday morning, after speaking to investors over the past 24 hours, Ives said it was a confusing time for Wall Street tech backers trying to "discern the poker game in the Beltway and how this will truly impact the AI Revolution buildout." "Putting all the pieces together we believe Big Tech capex growth rate now peaks in 2027 vs our previous view that would not happen until 2028/2029," he said. Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC . CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue. Meta seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps. Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station. Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap after midterms. Blue Origin pushes launch to January 2027 as it races to rebuild damaged launchpad. Elsewhere in midterm-land, it's not just data centers in the crosshairs. Democrats' sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, my colleague Tanaya Macheel writes. The result? It could usher in a more adversarial approach in Washington and push industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner, she says.

stories.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
stories.summary: “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Clément Delangue said of the need for open source AI.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
sources.text: Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami. “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.” Hugging Face is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught. Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too. Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.” In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said. Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems. Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users. Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks , a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI. Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future. “We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.” Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

sources.name: Tecmundo
sources.title: O risco da IA para a humanidade é ‘próximo de zero’, diz CEO da Hugging Face
sources.text: A inteligência artificial (IA) é perigosa em alguns aspectos, mas representa uma ameaça “próxima de zero” para a humanidade . A opinião é de Clément Delangue, CEO da Hugging Face. A plataforma é um repositório de códigos e modelos de IA, mais conhecida fora da indústria por ser até agora o alvo mais famoso de um agente rebelde da OpenAI. A opinião vai contra alguns pesquisadores do setor, que denunciam os possíveis riscos graves do crescimento acelerado da capacidade dessas ferramentas. Porém, o executivo crê que há “ muitos outros tópicos que podem destruir o mundo ” para além de um sistema automatizado. Delangue falou sobre o assunto durante um evento organizado pela Wired . No painel, o CEO defendeu ainda lutar pela criminalização de invasões cometidas por agentes de IA, mesmo os que estavam em ambientes de teste e “ saíram do controle ” dos responsáveis. “Ciberataques são ilegais, e considero fundamental garantir que ciberataques autônomos também sejam ilegais. Não queremos criar um cenário em que não haja responsabilização, em que ninguém responda” argumenta. Porém, a própria Hugging Face decidiu não processar ou denunciar a OpenAI após a tentativa de exploração de brechas. Atualmente de propriedade da Nvidia, a Hugging Face seguirá fomentando o mercado aberto de IA, para que modelos abertos e mais transparentes tenham cada vez mais espaço no mercado . Segundo Delangue, isso é essencial para evitar que a indústria da IA fique na mão de poucas empresas responsáveis — especialmente companhias que constroem modelos de ponta “ sob portas fechadas ” e em segredo, como é o caso da própria dona do ChatGPT. “É perfeitamente possível que acabemos em um mundo no qual apenas algumas empresas controlem a maior parte da IA. Existem tendências naturais muito fortes, já que elas acabam monopolizando talentos, poder computacional e capacidades”, alerta o executivo. A invasão da Hugging Face, segundo ele, é um exemplo disso: a companhia adotou um modelo aberto chinês, o GLM-5.2, para investigar e restringir os efeitos da invasão sofrida. A ideia da companhia é permitir que cada vez mais pessoas tenham acesso a modelos customizados de IA, o que ajudaria na formação de um “ futuro tecnológico mais democrático ”.
